name: Zanaki
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: For example, in Zanaki some speakers make use of regular penultimate stress – possibly under Swahili influence – (the variant described in this chapter) while others have several contrasting lexical and grammatical tone patterns. [p. 7] ... Zanaki has regular penultimate stress in all Infinitive forms (15). (15) Zanaki ɔkʊ['βɔha 'to close' oku['sɜkjɜ 'to try' oku[sɜ'kiɾjɜ 'to help' ɔkʊ[βɔhɛ'ɾɛɾa 'to tether' [p. 10]
new_statements.citation: Aunio, Lotta, Holly Robinson, Tim Roth, Oliver Stegen & John B. Walker. 2019. The Mara languages (JE40). In Mark Van de Velde, Koen Bostoen, Derek Nurse & Gérard Philippson (eds), The Bantu Languages, 2nd edn, 501-532. Abingdon: Routledge. DOI 10.4324/9781315755946-17 (author final draft from Helda, hdl:10138/322322)
new_statements.locator: §2.3 'Tone and syllable structure', preprint pp. 7 and 10 (PDF pp. 7, 10; example (15)); published pagination 501-532 not verified
new_statements.rule_in_words: For the (majority/described) Zanaki variety, word stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of the word (shown on infinitives: ɔkʊ-'βɔha, oku-sɜ'kiɾjɜ, ɔkʊ-βɔhɛ'ɾɛɾa), a Swahili-like pattern that has replaced lexical tone; a minority of speakers instead retain a lexical/grammatical H-tone system.
new_statements.exceptions: Speaker variation, not dialectal or age-based: some speakers keep a fairly complex tonal system (possibly four patterns for bisyllabic noun stems, p. 9) instead of penultimate stress; the authors call for more research on the variables. The corroborating SIL Orthography Statement (Robinson & Gray 2019, p. 11) repeats the same split and adds that tone has a low functional load.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; illustrated on infinitive verb forms (prefix + stem) in isolation; nouns described only as having 'shifted to penultimate stress' (p. 9) without examples. Chapter treats penultimate stress as replacing the lexical-tone system of other Mara languages.
new_statements.identity_note: Zanaki (Ikizanaki), Glottolog zana1238, ISO zak, Guthrie JE44 (Aunio et al. 2019 Table 1). The statement describes the majority/described variant with Swahili-like penultimate stress; the same sources report a co-existing tonal variant among some speakers (not dialectal). Not to be confused with Ikizu-Sizaki (ikiz1238) or Nata (JE45).
